newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kia seen staying as independent carmaker.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kia seen staying as independent carmaker.

text.p: South Korea's troubled Kia Group, supported by conglomerates that want to maintain the industrial status quo, will likely stave off a bid by its creditors to have Kia sell off its automaking flagship to a third party, analysts said on Sunday.

They said the group would benefit from intensive manoeuvring by the country's top conglomerates, or chaebol, to prevent Kia Motors Corp ending up in the hands of their rivals and from political pressures ahead of presidential elections in December.
Some economists have said a third-party takeover of Kia Motors could speed up the restructuring of the nation's automobile industry, which faces the threat of overcapacity.
"What ought to be done logically is one thing, and what is going to happen is another," said Chang Choong-rynn, a car industry analyst at Daewoo Securities.

"There are many obstacles for a third-party takeover," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of the Daewoo Research Institute. "Other conglomerates are strongly opposed to a change in the status quo in the industry and the ranking of chaebols."

Kia has maintained a tough stance against creditors, wielding a warning by top conglomerates that the acquisition of the third-largest carmaker in South Korea by one of their rivals could threaten their position and power.
Kia recorded annual sales of 6.61 trillion won ($7.4 billion) in calendar 1996, up from 5.69 trillion in 1995.
The Kia Group, the eighth-largest conglomerate, has rejected a call by creditors for its top executives to resign, a move widely seen as the first step towards a third-party takeover.

"Hyundai and Daewoo may cooperate to help Kia, but their ultimate intention is not owning Kia Motors but preventing a takeover by any of their rivals," said Sohn Jong-won, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.

Sohn was referring to the surprise agreement last week by the country's two largest carmakers -- Hyundai Motor Co and Daewoo Motor Co -- that they planned to inject cash into Kia's troubled steelmaking unit Kia Steel Co.
Under the agreement, Hyundai, Daewoo and Kia Motors would form a consortium with equal stakes in Kia Steel.
Facing tough resistance by Kia, creditor banks refused for the second time on Friday to begin discussing how to implement a July 15 decision to protect Kia from collapsing.
Their next meeting is set for Monday.
Creditors prefer a takeover of Kia by a healthy business group.
"Banks seem to believe a takeover would make it easier for them to get their loans repaid without having to assume any big losses," said Huh Ghang, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Out of its total debts of 9.54 trillion won, the Kia Group owed 5.48 trillion won to banks at the end of May, according to Korea Federation of Banks statistics.
Corporate analysts said that with no suitors actively pursuing Kia Motors the government was expected to pressure creditor banks to compromise.

"The government would not want political fallouts from the Kia saga in the run-up to the presidential election," said one analyst who asked not to be identified. "It would like to settle the issue as soon as possible."

Daewoo Securities' Chang said he expected Kia to try to make its self-rescue plans more attractive, while standing firm on the future of its automaking flagship. "In the end, creditors will find no choice but to accept the group's stance."
On Wednesday Kia announced a plan to cut the number of its domestic units to five from the current 28 through sell-offs, mergers and spin-offs.
It also said its other automaking unit, Asia Motors Corp, would sell off part of its assets before being absorbed by Kia Motors to serve as assembly plants.
(Conversion: $1 = 890.80 won)
